entries.answer: The forgetting curve is the rate at which unused memories decay, and the finding is that the drop is fast at first and then flattens, so most of what is learned is gone within a day and the remainder persists for a long time. What makes the curve useful is that reviewing resets the position without resetting the shape, so each repetition makes the next one cheaper. That is the whole basis of spaced study, and it is why a single review session does so little.

entries.answer: A mnemonic is a device that makes something easier to remember by attaching it to something already known, and the oldest form is a rhyme. It works for lists that are hard to order otherwise, so the order of the planets or the cranial nerves, and it is close to useless for anything requiring understanding. Its limitation is capacity: a mnemonic helps recall an item but does not explain why it is true, so it is a supplement rather than a replacement for learning the thing.

patterns: how many items can you hold
entries.answer: Working memory is the small amount held and manipulated at once, and it is the bottleneck for almost every hard task, since you cannot reason over material you are not holding. Its capacity is famously small, around four items, though chunking lets a trained person hold far more by treating groups as single objects. This is why a phone number is harder than a familiar phone number, and why experts appear to remember more simply because their chunks are larger.

entries.answer: Encoding is the process of turning something into a form that can be stored, and it is where most learning is actually lost. Material that is understood can still fail to encode if it is encoded in a form you will never retrieve, which is the reason a shelf of unlabelled boxes is not a memory aid. Depth of processing is the reliable predictor of retention, so asking why something is true encodes better than repeating that it is.

entries.answer: Retention is how long something stays available, and it is the outcome most people mean by learning a thing, so it is worth separating from the other two parts. Acquisition is getting it in, retention is keeping it, and retrieval is finding it, and a failure at any one looks identical from outside. The clinically important fact is that forgetting is not loss of the memory but loss of the route to it, so overlearning and varied practice both work by adding routes rather than by preventing decay.
